Personal project · Embedded systems

A synthesizer you play by touch

A digital synthesizer built on an STM32-based microcontroller, played with custom membrane potentiometers and capacitive touch pads.

Diego Becerra Fuentes · 05/2026 · Continuation of the membrane potentiometer project

Try it: interactive simulation

A simplified single-voice version of the instrument. Drag across the strip to slide the pitch, and use the dials below. The 12 capacitive pads are replaced by the keys shown on the pads below, which you can click, tap or press on your keyboard. Sound starts after your first touch.

Touch the strip to play

Each pad shows the interval it adds above the strip’s note (an arrow means below). The three left columns each play one chord note, and the three pads in a column shift it by a semitone up, none and a semitone down (top to bottom). The right column (4, R, F) switches between the sets of intervals, so the labels change when you hold one. The highlighted keys (Q, W, E) play each chord note at its unshifted interval.

Introduction

As a mechatronics engineer I work at the meeting point of mechanics, electronics and software. After a few years of studying each of them separately, I wanted a project where all of them had to work together, so I decided to build a digital synthesizer that is played through touch.

A synthesizer is an instrument that makes sound electronically. Its core is made of oscillators, which generate a raw periodic waveform, and filters, which shape its tone. Both can be analog (built from continuous circuits) or digital (computed as numbers by a processor). This one is fully digital.

Design

The brain of the instrument is the Daisy Seed, a small audio-oriented development board built around an STM32H7 ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller. It comes with a high-quality stereo audio codec, plenty of memory (including 64 MB of external SDRAM) and an Arduino-compatible toolchain, which makes it ideal for real-time sound synthesis.

Physically, the project is centered on a single main PCB that covers most of the instrument. It contains power, logic, amplification and the input devices in separate zones, and only the input devices are reachable by the user. The full list of components is:

  • 1 Daisy Seed microcontroller
  • 1 PAM8403 class-D amplifier board
  • 1 MPR121 capacitive touch sensor
  • 1 CD74HC4067 16-channel multiplexer
  • 3 custom membrane potentiometers
  • 16 10 kΩ potentiometers
  • 1 headphone jack
  • 2 6 mm audio jacks
  • 1 indicator LED
  • Switches, resistors and capacitors

Two kinds of touch

What makes this synthesizer special is that it uses both resistive and capacitive touch sensing. A membrane potentiometer is a strip with a resistive track under a flexible conductive layer. Pressing it creates a contact point, and the voltage at that point tells you how far along the strip you are touching, so it works like a slider you operate with your finger. A capacitive touch sensor measures the tiny change in capacitance that a finger causes on a copper pad. The MPR121 does this for 12 pads at once and reports each one over I²C.

I am a violin player, and I wanted to recreate the feeling of sliding a finger along a string and hearing the pitch change continuously. The inspiration was the Ondes Martenot, an early electronic instrument from 1928 in which the player slides a ring along a wire to change pitch continuously, like a string, while the other hand shapes the volume. Two strips control two different voices and a third strip controls the volume.

I also wanted the polyphony of a piano. The touch pads play notes at fixed intervals from the main note, so that chords can be built with a single hand. This idea comes from the Omnichord.

Both analog and digital parts share the board. Although the Daisy Seed provides separate analog and digital rails, I used a common ground plane for both, because it is simpler and the manuals recommended it. The only place without a ground plane is around the capacitive pads and the traces that connect them to the MPR121, because copper nearby adds parasitic capacitance and would reduce the sensor’s sensitivity to a finger.

The board was also designed so it could be split: the section with the multiplexer and the potentiometers was meant to sit on a raised surface, but given its size it was cheaper to order everything as one PCB.

Construction

The enclosure is made from 3 mm MDF panels with a simple box construction, inspired by classic Stylophones. Below is the 3D model of the MDF layers that frame the membrane strip, in a light wood color. Drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom.

· Loading model…

On the back, the synthesizer has a power jack that needs a steady 12 V DC. A 2-pole, 2-throw switch with a center-off position chooses where the audio goes: through the amplifier to the built-in speakers, or to two separate mono output jacks, one per voice. In the center position the output is muted.

Programming

I programmed everything in the Arduino IDE for simplicity, and the Daisy Seed still gave me the performance I needed. The first step was testing every input: the membrane potentiometers, the capacitive pads through the MPR121, the potentiometers wired through the multiplexer, and the digital switches.

The membrane strips and the capacitive pads were the tricky ones. I had already modeled the non-linear output of the strips, but computing that model continuously was unnecessarily heavy for the microcontroller. Instead, I measured the sensor’s output at equal steps along its length and split the points into a linear section and a quadratic section. The code just picks the right section and evaluates a simple polynomial to get the touched position.

The capacitive pads follow the same philosophy. At startup the code waits two seconds and stores each pad’s resting value. After that it compares every new reading against that baseline, averages the last ten differences to filter noise, and only counts a pad as touched after it stays above a threshold for several consecutive loops. That avoids false triggers.

With the inputs working, I built the outputs. An oscillator is a block of code that keeps a phase value, advances it by a small step on every audio sample, and turns that phase into a sample of a sine, square, triangle or sawtooth wave. The step size sets the frequency. The touched position becomes a pitch with the equal-temperament relation, where every 12 semitones double the frequency:

f=f0·2b+n12·2o−1with f0 = 32.7 Hz (the note C1)

Here b is the beginning note (0 to 11 semitones above C), o is the octave (3 to 6) and n is the distance in semitones (0 to 12) that comes from the touched position. Inside the oscillator, the phase φ advances on every audio sample and the output is read from it:

φ[k]=(φ[k−1]+2πffs)mod2πy[k]=A·sin(φ[k])with sample rate fs = 48 kHz and amplitude A; the other waves replace sin with a square, triangle or sawtooth of φ

The first strip controls the first voice. The second voice is the second strip combined with the extra chord notes from the capacitive pads.

With 16 potentiometers available, I split them evenly between the two voices, and then again into four dials that shape the basic wave and four that control effects. The four wave controls are:

  • Beginning note: the strip covers one octave, and this dial chooses which note of the scale it starts on.
  • Note octave: chooses the octave where that scale begins. Together with the first dial it fixes the exact starting note.
  • Wave type: sine, square, triangle or sawtooth.
  • Note quantizing: how discrete the pitch is, from a free slide to locked semitones, so you can trade sliding for staying in tune.

Starting note and octave

Wave types

Each button plays A3 (220 Hz) with a different waveform. The sawtooth is the brightest, the sine the purest.

Note quantizing

Touch position along the strip (horizontal) against the resulting pitch in semitones (vertical). At 0 the pitch is continuous; at 1 it snaps to the nearest semitone.

The four effects are:

  • Reverb: simulates the echoes of a room. I used the ReverbSc algorithm from DaisySP, with a long decay and a bright tone.
  • Delay: repeats the sound after a short time, and the repeats are fed back at lower volume, giving an echo trail.
  • Tremolo: a slow, periodic change of volume.
  • Vibrato: a slow, periodic change of pitch, like the finger wobble of a violinist.

Tremolo and vibrato

Move the sliders while it plays to hear the difference.

Tremolo changes the wave’s height, vibrato changes how tightly the wave is packed. The pitch change is exaggerated in the drawing so you can see it; the sound plays both effects at their real size.

Delay and reverb need memory. A delay is a circular buffer: each audio sample is written at the current position and read back from a position that is a fixed number of samples behind, which sets the delay time. Two seconds of audio at 48 kHz is 96,000 floating-point samples, around 384 kB, which does not fit comfortably in the microcontroller’s fast internal RAM, so the buffer is placed in the external SDRAM. The reverb uses the same kind of large buffers.

View the full source code (Arduino / DaisyDuino)

#include "DaisyDuino.h"
#include <Wire.h>
#include "Adafruit_MPR121.h"


using namespace daisysp;

// ===== DELAY (SDRAM) =====
#define MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES (48000 * 2) // 2 seconds

DSY_SDRAM_BSS float delayBuffer[MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES];

int writeIndex = 0;
int delaySamples = 24000; // ~0.5 sec default

float delayFeedback = 0.4f;

// Delay control
float delaySend1 = 0.0f;     // OSC1
float delaySendAll = 0.0f;   // others

// ===== REVERB =====
ReverbSc reverb;

// Optional: large SDRAM buffer (future-proof if you expand)
DSY_SDRAM_BSS float reverbBuffer[48000 * 2];

DaisyHardware hw;

// ================= ORIGINAL OSC =================
Oscillator osc1;
Oscillator osc2;

// ================= NEW OSC (MPR121) =================
Oscillator osc3;
Oscillator osc4;
Oscillator osc5;

// ================= MPR121 =================
Adafruit_MPR121 cap = Adafruit_MPR121();

uint16_t restValues[12];
bool calibrated = false;

#define NUM_SAMPLES 10
int16_t history[12][NUM_SAMPLES];
uint8_t indexPos = 0;
bool bufferFilled = false;

uint8_t touchCount[12];
bool touched[12];

int ch1 = 0, ch2 = 0, ch3 = 0;
int ch1b = 0, ch2b = 0, ch3b = 0;
int ch1p = 0, ch2p = 0, ch3p = 0;

// ===== MUX =====
const int S0 = 2;
const int S1 = 3;
const int S2 = 4;
const int S3 = 5;
const int SIG_PIN = A3;

// Pots
const int pot0 = A0;
const int pot1 = A1;
const int pot2 = A2;

// Digital inputs
const int pin1 = A4;
const int pin2 = A5;
const int pin3 = A6;
const int pin4 = A7;

// Variables
float d0 = 0;
float new_d0 = 0;
float d1, d2;

float revSend1 = 0.0f;     // OSC1 reverb send
float revSendAll = 0.0f;   // others reverb send

// ===== TREMOLO =====
float tremRate1 = 0.0f;     // OSC1 rate
float tremRateAll = 0.0f;   // others rate

float tremPhase1 = 0.0f;
float tremPhaseAll = 0.0f;

// ===== VIBRATO =====
float vibRate1 = 0.0f;     // OSC1 rate (MUX 1)
float vibRateAll = 0.0f;   // others rate (MUX 15)

float vibPhase1 = 0.0f;
float vibPhaseAll = 0.0f;

float n1, n2;
float held_n2 = 0;

int t0, t1, t2;

int base1, base2;
int octave1, octave2;
int wave1, wave2;

float freq1, freq2;

#define SAMPLE_RATE 48000

// ================= LOUDNESS =================
float LoudnessComp(float freq)
{
  if (freq < 200.0) return 1.5;
  else if (freq < 1000.0) return 1.2;
  else if (freq < 3000.0) return 1.0;
  else if (freq < 6000.0) return 0.8;
  else return 0.6;
}

// ================= AUDIO CALLBACK =================
void AudioCallback(float **in, float **out, size_t size)
{
  for (size_t i = 0; i < size; i++)
{
// ===== TREMOLO LFO =====
float rate1 = tremRate1 * 12.0f;
float rateAll = tremRateAll * 12.0f;

// ===== VIBRATO LFO =====
float vibRateHz1 = vibRate1 * 12.0f;     // adjust max speed here
float vibRateHzAll = vibRateAll * 12.0f;

float vib1 = 0.0f;
float vibAll = 0.0f;

// --- OSC1 vibrato ---
float baselineSemi = -0.5f;   // ⭐ center of (-1 → 0)
float depthSemi = 0.5f;       // ⭐ half range

if (vibRate1 < 0.05f)   // ⭐ POT threshold (adjust feel here)
{
    vibPhase1 = 0.0f;
    vib1 = 1.0f;        // ⭐ TRUE BYPASS (no detune)
}
else
{
    vibPhase1 += vibRateHz1 / SAMPLE_RATE;
    if (vibPhase1 >= 1.0f) vibPhase1 -= 1.0f;

    float lfo = sinf(TWO_PI * vibPhase1); // -1 → 1

    float semitoneOffset = lfo * depthSemi;   // ⭐ CENTERED at 0

    vib1 = powf(2.0f, semitoneOffset / 12.0f);
}

// --- OTHER OSC vibrato ---
float baselineSemiAll = -0.5f;
float depthSemiAll = 0.5f;

if (vibRateAll < 0.05f)
{
    vibPhaseAll = 0.0f;
    vibAll = 1.0f;   // ⭐ TRUE BYPASS
}
else
{
    vibPhaseAll += vibRateHzAll / SAMPLE_RATE;
    if (vibPhaseAll >= 1.0f) vibPhaseAll -= 1.0f;

    float lfo = sinf(TWO_PI * vibPhaseAll);

    float semitoneOffset = lfo * depthSemiAll;

    vibAll = powf(2.0f, semitoneOffset / 12.0f);
}

// If rate is very small → disable tremolo
float trem1, tremAll;

float baselineTrem = 0.65f;   // ⭐ center of 0.3–1.0
float depthTrem = 0.35f;      // ⭐ half range

if (tremRate1 < 0.05f)
{
    tremPhase1 = 0.0f;
    trem1 = 1.0f;   // ⭐ TRUE BYPASS (no volume drop)
}
else
{
    tremPhase1 += rate1 / SAMPLE_RATE;
    if (tremPhase1 >= 1.0f) tremPhase1 -= 1.0f;

    float lfo = sinf(TWO_PI * tremPhase1); // -1 → 1

    trem1 = 1.0f + (lfo * depthTrem);
}



float baselineTremAll = 0.65f;
float depthTremAll = 0.35f;

if (tremRateAll < 0.05f)
{
    tremPhaseAll = 0.0f;
    tremAll = 1.0f;   // ⭐ TRUE BYPASS
}
else
{
    tremPhaseAll += rateAll / SAMPLE_RATE;
    if (tremPhaseAll >= 1.0f) tremPhaseAll -= 1.0f;

    float lfo = sinf(TWO_PI * tremPhaseAll);

    tremAll = 1.0f + (lfo * depthTremAll);
}

    float sig1 = 0.0f;
    float sig2 = 0.0f;

    float rev_in = 0.0f;
    float rev_l, rev_r;

    float delay_in = 0.0f;
    float delay_out = delayBuffer[(writeIndex - delaySamples + MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES) % MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES];

    // ===== ORIGINAL ENGINE =====
    int mode = digitalRead(pin3);
    bool allowSound = false;

    if (mode == 0)
    {
        if (t0 == 1 && (t1 == 1 || t2 == 1))
            allowSound = true;
    }
    else
    {
        if (t1 == 1 || t2 == 1)
            allowSound = true;
    }

    // -------- OSC1 --------
    if (allowSound && t1 == 1)
    {
        osc1.SetFreq(freq1 * vib1);

        float gain = 1.0;
        switch (wave1)
        {
            case 1: gain = 0.8; break;
            case 2: gain = 0.15; break;
            case 3: gain = 0.95; break;
            case 4: gain = 0.2; break;
        }

        float s = osc1.Process() * (d0 / 4.0) * gain * LoudnessComp(freq1) * trem1;
        sig1 += s;

        rev_in += s * revSend1;
        delay_in += s * delaySend1;
    }

    // -------- OSC2 --------
    bool AD7 = digitalRead(pin4);
    bool mprActive = (ch1p || ch2p || ch3p);
    bool playOsc2 = (t2 == 1) || (AD7 == 1 && mprActive);

    if (allowSound && playOsc2)
    {
        osc2.SetFreq(freq2 * vibAll);

        float gain = 1.0;
        switch (wave2)
        {
            case 1: gain = 0.8; break;
            case 2: gain = 0.15; break;
            case 3: gain = 0.95; break;
            case 4: gain = 0.2; break;
        }

        float s = osc2.Process() * (d0 / 4.0) * gain * LoudnessComp(freq2) * tremAll;
        sig2 += s;

        rev_in += s * revSendAll;
        delay_in += s * delaySendAll;
    }

    // ===== MPR121 OSC =====
float m1 = 0.0f;

if (ch1p)
{
    float baseFreq = freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch1 / 12.0f);
    osc3.SetFreq(baseFreq * vibAll);   // ⭐ INSERT THIS LINE

    m1 = osc3.Process() * (d0 / 4.0f) * LoudnessComp(baseFreq) * tremAll;
}

float m2 = 0.0f;

if (ch2p)
{
    float baseFreq = freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch2 / 12.0f);
    osc4.SetFreq(baseFreq * vibAll);   // ⭐ INSERT HERE

    m2 = osc4.Process() * (d0 / 4.0f) * LoudnessComp(baseFreq) * tremAll;
}

float m3 = 0.0f;

if (ch3p)
{
    float baseFreq = freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch3 / 12.0f);
    osc5.SetFreq(baseFreq * vibAll);   // ⭐ INSERT HERE

    m3 = osc5.Process() * (d0 / 4.0f) * LoudnessComp(baseFreq) * tremAll;
}


    float mixMPR = (m1 + m2 + m3) * 0.3f;

    sig1 += mixMPR;
    sig2 += mixMPR;

    rev_in += mixMPR * revSendAll;
    delay_in += mixMPR * delaySendAll;

    // ===== DELAY WRITE (with feedback) =====
    delayBuffer[writeIndex] = delay_in + delay_out * delayFeedback;

    writeIndex++;
    if (writeIndex >= MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES)
        writeIndex = 0;

    // ===== REVERB =====
    reverb.Process(rev_in, rev_in, &rev_l, &rev_r);

    // ===== FINAL MIX =====
    float finalL = sig1 + rev_l + delay_out;
    float finalR = sig2 + rev_r + delay_out;

    out[0][i] = finalL;
    out[1][i] = finalR;
}
}

// ================= MUX =================
void selectChannel(int ch)
{
  digitalWrite(S0, ch & 1);
  digitalWrite(S1, (ch >> 1) & 1);
  digitalWrite(S2, (ch >> 2) & 1);
  digitalWrite(S3, (ch >> 3) & 1);
}

int readMux(int ch)
{
  selectChannel(ch);
  delayMicroseconds(50);
  analogRead(SIG_PIN);
  return analogRead(SIG_PIN);
}

float snapValue(float x, float snap)
{
  float nearest = round(x);
  float diff = x - nearest;
  float deadband = 0.5 * snap;

  if (abs(diff) < deadband)
    return nearest;
  else
    return x;
}

// ================= SETUP =================
void setup()
{
  Serial.begin(9600);
  analogReadResolution(12);

  reverb.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
reverb.SetFeedback(0.85f);   // decay time
reverb.SetLpFreq(18000.0f);  // brightness


  hw = DAISY.init(DAISY_SEED, AUDIO_SR_48K);

  osc1.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
  osc2.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
  osc3.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
  osc4.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
  osc5.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);

  osc1.SetAmp(1.0f);
  osc2.SetAmp(1.0f);
  osc3.SetAmp(1.0f);
  osc4.SetAmp(1.0f);
  osc5.SetAmp(1.0f);

// ===== CLEAR DELAY BUFFER =====
for (int i = 0; i < MAX_DELAY_SAMPLES; i++)
{
    delayBuffer[i] = 0.0f;
}

// Reset index
writeIndex = 0;

// ===== START AUDIO =====

  DAISY.begin(AudioCallback);

  pinMode(S0, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(S1, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(S2, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(S3, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(SIG_PIN, INPUT);

  pinMode(pin1, INPUT);
  pinMode(pin2, INPUT);
  pinMode(pin3, INPUT);
  pinMode(pin4, INPUT);

  reverb.Init(SAMPLE_RATE);
  reverb.SetFeedback(0.85f);   // decay time
  reverb.SetLpFreq(18000.0f);  // brightness



  Wire.begin(29, 28);

  if (!cap.begin(0x5A)) {
    Serial.println("MPR121 not found");
    while (1);
  }
}

// ================= LOOP =================
void loop()
{ 

revSend1 = readMux(2) / 4095.0f;
revSendAll = readMux(9) / 4095.0f;
delaySend1  = readMux(3) / 4095.0f;
delaySendAll = readMux(14) / 4095.0f;

// ===== TREMOLO CONTROL =====
tremRate1 = readMux(0) / 4095.0f;
tremRateAll = readMux(8) / 4095.0f;

// ===== VIBRATO CONTROL =====
vibRate1 = readMux(1) / 4095.0f;
vibRateAll = readMux(15) / 4095.0f;

  int A0_val = analogRead(pot0);
  int A1_val = analogRead(pot1);
  int A2_val = analogRead(pot2);

  t0 = (A0_val < 160) ? 0 : 1;
  t1 = (A1_val < 170) ? 0 : 1;
  t2 = (A2_val < 170) ? 0 : 1;

  if (A0_val < 260)
    new_d0 = 0;
  else
    new_d0 = 0.000403234 * A0_val - 0.106866;

  if (t0 == 1)
    d0 = new_d0;

  if (A1_val > 3620)
    d1 = 12;
  else if (A1_val > 1660)
    d1 = -0.000000629046 * A1_val * A1_val + 0.00636242 * A1_val - 2.810773;
  else if (A1_val >= 275)
    d1 = 0.00443316 * A1_val - 1.334994;
  else
    d1 = 0;

  if (A2_val > 3620)
    d2 = 12;
  else if (A2_val > 1660)
    d2 = -0.000000629046 * A2_val * A2_val + 0.00636242 * A2_val - 2.810773;
  else if (A2_val >= 275)
    d2 = 0.00443316 * A2_val - 1.334994;
  else
    d2 = 0;

  int state1 = digitalRead(pin1);
  int state2 = digitalRead(pin2);

  float raw_n1 = (state1 == 0) ? d1 : d1 * 2;
  float raw_n2 = (state2 == 0) ? d2 : d2 * 2;

  float snap1 = readMux(5) / 4095.0;
  float snap2 = readMux(13) / 4095.0;

  n1 = snapValue(raw_n1, snap1);

  if (t2 == 1)
    held_n2 = snapValue(raw_n2, snap2);

  n2 = held_n2;

  base1 = map(readMux(6), 0, 4095, 0, 12);
  base2 = map(readMux(11), 0, 4095, 0, 12);

  octave1 = map(readMux(7), 0, 4095, 3, 7);
  octave2 = map(readMux(12), 0, 4095, 3, 7);

  wave1 = map(readMux(4), 0, 4095, 1, 5);
  wave2 = map(readMux(10), 0, 4095, 1, 5);

  if (base1 == 12) base1 = 11;
  if (base2 == 12) base2 = 11;
  if (octave1 == 7) octave1 = 6;
  if (octave2 == 7) octave2 = 6;
  if (wave1 == 5) wave1 = 4;
  if (wave2 == 5) wave2 = 4;

  switch (wave1)
  {
    case 1: osc1.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SIN); break;
    case 2: osc1.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SQUARE); break;
    case 3: osc1.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_TRI); break;
    case 4: osc1.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SAW); break;
  }

  switch (wave2)
  {
    case 1: osc2.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SIN); break;
    case 2: osc2.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SQUARE); break;
    case 3: osc2.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_TRI); break;
    case 4: osc2.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SAW); break;
  }

  switch (wave2)
  {
    case 1:
      osc3.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SIN);
      osc4.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SIN);
      osc5.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SIN);
      break;
    case 2:
      osc3.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SQUARE);
      osc4.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SQUARE);
      osc5.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SQUARE);
      break;
    case 3:
      osc3.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_TRI);
      osc4.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_TRI);
      osc5.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_TRI);
      break;
    case 4:
      osc3.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SAW);
      osc4.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SAW);
      osc5.SetWaveform(Oscillator::WAVE_SAW);
      break;
  }

  freq1 = (32.7 * pow(2, base1 / 12.0)) *
          pow(2, octave1 - 1) *
          pow(2, n1 / 12.0);

  freq2 = (32.7 * pow(2, base2 / 12.0)) *
          pow(2, octave2 - 1) *
          pow(2, n2 / 12.0);

  if (!calibrated) {
    delay(2000);
    for (uint8_t i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
      restValues[i] = cap.filteredData(i);
      touchCount[i] = 0;
      touched[i] = false;
    }
    calibrated = true;
  }

  for (uint8_t i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
    uint16_t current = cap.filteredData(i);
    int16_t diff = restValues[i] - current;
    history[i][indexPos] = abs(diff);
  }

  indexPos++;
  if (indexPos >= NUM_SAMPLES) {
    indexPos = 0;
    bufferFilled = true;
  }

  for (uint8_t i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
    int32_t sum = 0;
    uint8_t count = bufferFilled ? NUM_SAMPLES : indexPos;
    if (count == 0) count = 1;

    for (uint8_t j = 0; j < count; j++) {
      sum += history[i][j];
    }

    int16_t avg = sum / count;

    if (avg > 2) touchCount[i]++;
    else {
      touchCount[i] = 0;
      touched[i] = false;
    }

    if (touchCount[i] > 8) touched[i] = true;
  }

  if (touched[9]) { ch1b = -12; ch2b = -8; ch3b = -5; }
  else if (touched[10]) { ch1b = -7; ch2b = -3; ch3b = 5; }
  else if (touched[11]) { ch1b = -4; ch2b = 3; ch3b = 8; }
  else { ch1b = 4; ch2b = 7; ch3b = 12; }

  if (touched[6]) ch1 = ch1b + 1;
  else if (touched[7]) ch1 = ch1b;
  else if (touched[8]) ch1 = ch1b - 1;

  if (touched[3]) ch2 = ch2b + 1;
  else if (touched[4]) ch2 = ch2b;
  else if (touched[5]) ch2 = ch2b - 1;

  if (touched[0]) ch3 = ch3b + 1;
  else if (touched[1]) ch3 = ch3b;
  else if (touched[2]) ch3 = ch3b - 1;

  ch1p = (touched[6] || touched[7] || touched[8]);
  ch2p = (touched[3] || touched[4] || touched[5]);
  ch3p = (touched[0] || touched[1] || touched[2]);

// Read MUX for vibrato control (channel 15 for all oscillators except osc1)


float vibControlAll = readMux(15);  

// Map to LFO frequency range (adjust as needed)
float lfoFreqAll = map(vibControlAll, 0, 1023, 1, 10);  

// Generate LFO (example using millis)
float t = millis() / 1000.0f;
float lfoAll = (sin(2.0f * PI * lfoFreqAll * t) + 1.0f) * 0.5f;  

// Convert to pitch modulation: 0 → -1 semitone, 1 → 0 semitone
float vibAll = pow(2.0f, (lfoAll - 1.0f) / 12.0f);

 osc3.SetFreq(freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch1 / 12.0f) * vibAll);
osc4.SetFreq(freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch2 / 12.0f) * vibAll);
osc5.SetFreq(freq2 * pow(2.0f, ch3 / 12.0f) * vibAll);

  delay(10);
}

Results

Conclusion

This project was the culmination of the skills I have developed in embedded systems, CAD design, subtractive manufacturing, PCB design and microcontroller programming. It was the first time that I carried one instrument through every stage, from an idea about how a violin feels, through schematics, a custom board, laser-cut enclosure and real-time firmware, to a finished object that makes music.

Along the way I learned practical lessons: that measuring a sensor and fitting a simple curve can beat an exact model on a small processor, that grounding and layout matter for capacitive sensing, and that a design decision like putting everything on one PCB has cost, assembly and usability consequences. The synthesizer is not finished. There is room for better filters and more voices, but it already does what I wanted it to do: it lets me slide a finger and hear the pitch follow.
